title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks
author: Jordan Kim
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's SRE guidance for defining and operating service-level objectives (SLOs), managing error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended for on-call engineers, SREs, service owners, and platform teams.

Key principles
- Prioritize user-visible reliability: SLOs should reflect end-user impact, not internal metrics only.
- Use error budgets to enable safe change: increase velocity while bounding risk.
- Automate measurement and remediation where possible.
- Keep runbooks concise, stepwise, and tested (game-days).
- Conduct blameless, timely incident reviews with clear follow-ups.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Purpose and scope
- SLOs define acceptable levels of service from the customer perspective (latency, availability, correctness). Each public-facing API and major internal dependency must have an SLO.
- Services covered in this doc: inference API, streaming responses, model catalog, embedding service, routing layer, and cache layer.

SLO taxonomy (examples)
- Inference API (text generation): Availability SLO: 99.95% measured over a 30-day window for HTTP 2xx responses; P99 latency SLO: P99 < 800ms for payload size <= 512 tokens, 30-day window.
- Streaming endpoints: Availability 99.9% (7-day window) for session continuity; Per-chunk latency P95 < 200ms.
- Embeddings: Availability 99.99% (30-day window), P99 latency < 250ms.
- Model catalog: Staleness SLO: model metadata updates propagated within 5 minutes 99.9% of the time.

Measurement and instrumentation
- Source of truth: the SRE metrics pipeline (Prometheus -> Cortex -> aggregated metrics in Grafana/Tempo).
- SLOs must use end-to-end synthetic transactions (canary requests) and real traffic error/latency buckets. Synthetic checks must run from multiple regions.
- Error classification: map HTTP 5xx, model-runtime errors (OOM, out-of-memory), explicit model failure payloads, and streaming disconnects to the error budget where they are user-visible. Internal transient retries that are not user-visible should be visible in monitoring but excluded from SLO calculations after justification documented in related_pages.

Windows and burn-rate
- Rolling windows: prefer a 30-day primary window and a 7-day fast-moving window for burn-rate detection on high-risk services.
- Error budget policies:
  - If burn rate (30-day) exceeds 1.5x expected at any point in the 7-day window, trigger a burn-rate alert.
  - If 7-day burn rate exceeds 3x and projected budget exhaustion within 48 hours, start change freeze and incident postmortem.

Alerting and governance
- Alert tiers:
  - Page (P0): projected error budget exhaustion within 24h or SLO breach in progress. Notifies SRE and service owners.
  - Pager (P1): sustained elevated burn rate that could exhaust budget within 72h. Notifies SRE rotation.
  - Ticket (P2): low-priority burn rate increases; routed to product/engineers queue.
- Governance actions on budget depletion:
  1. Inform product and stakeholders with the current runbook actions.
  2. Reduce risky rollouts and disable non-essential experiments.
  3. Engage incident response if user impact is significant.

SLO ownership and reviews
- Every SLO must list an owner in the service's Confluence page and be reviewed quarterly. Owners are responsible for instrumenting metrics, owning dashboards, and participating in postmortems where SLOs were affected.

2) Capacity Planning and Headroom

Goals and cadence
- Ensure sufficient capacity for expected load plus headroom for spikes, model upgrades, and region failover. Review forecasting monthly and commit capacity quarterly.

Inputs to forecasts
- Traffic growth (weekly and monthly trends by route), model size changes (larger models increase memory and GPU time), new feature rollouts, historical incident/traffic spike patterns, and committed customers (Dedicated/Private contracts).

Capacity model (high level)
- Inputs: QPS by route, average tokens per request, P95/P99 latency targets, model GPU memory footprint, batch sizing parameters, and availability SLO.
- Outputs: required GPU count by machine type, expected utilization, autoscaling policies, and reserve pools for canary/rollout bursts.

Headroom rules of thumb
- Production GPU clusters: target steady-state utilization between 50–70% for multicard workloads with latency SLOs. For high-throughput embedding-only pools, utilization up to 80% is permitted if P99 latency remains within SLOs.
- Reserve pool: maintain at least 10% of cluster capacity as instant-burst capacity across AZs for critical services (higher for high-risk model launches).

Autoscaling and burst policies
- Autoscaling triggers should be based on request queue length and real-time p99 latency signals, not only CPU/GPU utilization.
- Provide a warm-up capacity policy for scheduled model rollouts (pre-warm nodes and load them with traffic gradually).

Capacity testing and validation
- Run quarterly load tests that mimic production mixing of short and long generation requests with representative token distributions. Test model upgrades using canary traffic and validate SLOs before wider rollout.

3) Reliability Initiatives and OKRs

Program structure
- Initiatives are prioritized quarterly. Typical categories: latency reduction, SLO coverage expansion, caching improvements, autoscaling robustness, and cross-region failover.

Example initiatives (FY25 Q1)
- Continuous batching improvements: reduce per-token cost by 12% while preserving P99 latency.
- KV cache persistence: introduce checkpointing to speed cold starts and reduce cache-miss cascade failures.
- Fast-fail model fallback: automated routing to lighter quantized variant on memory pressure.

Metrics and success criteria
- Define measurable KPIs per initiative: e.g., delta in P99 latency, reduction in error budget burn, cost-per-inference, and rollback rate for model updates.

4) Incident Review Standards

Timing and cadence
- Postmortems must be opened within 48 hours of incident mitigation and finalized within 14 days. A one-week summary update is required for major incidents.

Template (required fields)
- Title (short):
- Severity: P0/P1/P2
- Date/time (start, mitigation, full restore)
- Impact summary (customer-visible effects)
- Detection mechanism (monitoring/alert/runbook)
- Timeline of events (chronological)
- Root cause analysis (technical causes and contributing process failures)
- Remediation and corrective actions (owner and due date)
- Customer communications and status page links
- Learnings and action verification plan

Blameless culture and verification
- Avoid person-level attribution in postmortems. Focus on systems and process improvements. Leadership must review and endorse corrective actions within one sprint. Implement follow-ups and verify within assigned due dates.

Example RCA brief
- Incident: P0 inference API outage due to model-serving memory leak.
- Root cause: new kernel change increased per-request tensor allocations; autorelease path was skipped under certain request sizes.
- Immediate remediation: roll back kernel change, scale replicas temporarily, enable aggressive GC.
- Long-term fix: enforce memory regression tests in CI and introduce heap profiling during canary runs.

5) Operational Tooling and Observability

Dashboards and key queries
- Required dashboards per service: SLO overview, latency heatmap by route and model, error-class breakdown, capacity/utilization, and queued-request distribution.
- Example Grafana query snippets (PromQL style):
  - Service availability: 1 - sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"inference\",status=~\"5..\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=\"inference\"}[5m]))
  - P99 latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"inference\"}[5m])) by (le))

Tracing and logs
- Traces must be sampled deterministically for high-volume routes (e.g., 1/1000) and fully captured for canary synthetic transactions. Include model-id and model-version as tags in spans.
- Structured logs with request_id, trace_id, model_id, GPU_id, and request_size are required for root-cause analysis.

Automated remediation hooks
- Integrate limited automatic mitigations: scale-up on queue-length spike, restart worker on detected OOM signature, and fallback to a secondary model variant on repeated model runtime errors. Automatic actions must open a ticket and annotate the relevant trace/alert.

6) SRE Runbooks (Canonical)

Runbook: High 5xx rate on inference API
- Scope: user-visible 5xxs for inference API route /v1/generate.
- Pre-reqs: access to Grafana, logs (Loki), tracing (Tempo), cluster admin RBAC, and deploy tooling.
- Steps:
  1. Confirm SLO and alert details, capture current burn rate and projected exhaustion.
  2. Identify error classes: use query by status and by model_id.
     - Loki query example: {app=\"inference\", route=\"/v1/generate\"} | json | status >= 500 | count_over_time(5m)
  3. Check recent deploys: pipeline ID and commit for the service in last 60 minutes. If a deploy correlates, roll back or trigger canary isolation.
  4. Inspect node health: OOMs, GPU driver resets, or elevated GPU temperature.
  5. If errors are model-runtime related, switch traffic to last-known-good model variant and notify owners.
  6. If errors are infrastructure related, increase replica count or fail over to another AZ/reserved pool.
  7. Create incident and follow incident review template.

Runbook: P99 latency regression for streaming
- Scope: P99 latency spike > 2x baseline for streaming chunk delivery.
- Steps:
  1. Verify route and affected regions.
  2. Inspect batching statistics: batch size distribution, average batch wait time.
     - Grafana panels: batch-size-by-model, avg-batch-wait-ms.
  3. If batching queues are long, trigger autoscaler to add warm nodes. Consider decreasing max_batch_wait_ms for critical routes.
  4. For model-level slowness, fallback to lighter quantized variant or serve from cached prefix if available.
  5. If network egress or CDN issues suspected, validate cross-region network metrics and CDN health page.

Runbook: Cluster out-of-capacity (GPU pool saturation)
- Steps:
  1. Verify utilization and queue length across pools.
  2. Move non-critical workloads to lower-priority pools or pause experiments.
  3. Redeploy hot-pools from reserved capacity or burst pool.
  4. If autoscaler cannot add nodes, escalate to infra SRE and follow cloud provider runbook for quota increases.

Runbook: Model load failure (OOM, initialization error)
- Steps:
  1. Check model loader logs for stack traces and failed allocations.
  2. If OOM on a single node, mark node as unschedulable for similar model sizes and drain.
  3. Fallback routing: route to lower-memory quantized variant or to Hosted fallback.
  4. Open bug with model-onboarding and mark model as failing in catalog until fixed.

Runbook testing and maintenance
- Runbooks must be exercised at least twice per year in game-days. Document results under related_pages. Keep runbooks < 2 pages when printed. Annotate runbook changes with owner and date.

7) Roles, Ownership, and Escalation Paths

- SRE rotation: primary (page), secondary (notify), and tertiary (escalation) — pages are configured to include on-call engineers and service owners.
- Owners: every service SLO and runbook must list a service owner and an SRE contact.
- Escalation matrix: include phone and Slack escalation for P0s; follow on-call runbook for contact sequences.

Appendices

A) Example SLO table
| Service | Metric | Window | Target | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Inference API (/v1/generate) | Availability (2xx) | 30d | 99.95% | eng-inference-team |
| Streaming (sessions) | Session continuity | 7d | 99.9% | eng-inference-streaming |
| Embeddings API | Availability | 30d | 99.99% | eng-embeddings |

B) Useful playbook commands and snippets
- Inspect recent errors (Loki): loki query: '{app=\"inference\", route=\"/v1/generate\"} |= \"error\" | count_over_time(5m)'
- Check GPU driver resets (kubectl): kubectl get events --field-selector reason=GPUDriverReset -n inference
- Trigger canary rollback: infra-cli deploy rollback --service inference --to=previous --reason=\"SLO breach\"
